# FRA — Full Card Reference (Visual Grid)

*Every draftable FRA card (280 total) as a tile: image, 17Lands ratings, Draftsim grade /5, expert-guide notes, and an AI take. Ratings: 17Lands PremierDraft (1200-day sample). Generated by `build_card_reference.py`.*

**Legend** — **GIH** = Games-in-Hand WR (primary) · **IWD** = Improvement When Drawn (pp) · **ALSA** = Avg Last Seen At (lower = earlier) · **OH/GD** = Opening-Hand / Drawn WR · **Play** = play rate · **DS** = Draftsim grade /5 · **AZ** = MTG Arena Zone grade /5.  🤖 AI · 📝 Draftsim · 🅰 MTG Arena Zone.

> **Ordering:** cards within each colour are ranked by a combined **ALSA + play-rate** score (rank-average of the two), not by GIH WR. Both are populated by every draft — where the field takes a card, and how often it makes the deck — so together they track pick priority. A win rate answers a different question: which decks drafted the card.

**B/R is the consensus best pair** (most removal overall; no colour has more at common than black or red), and its one weakness is two-drop depth. **G/U is the consensus trap** — fewest removal spells of any pair, a six-mana signpost, and the Jace pieces it wants are contested by every other deck.

**Removal benchmarks:** Prophesied End ({1}{W} instant, destroys any creature — the best rate in the set), Last Gasp ({1}{B} −3/−3) and No Admittance ({1}{R} 3 damage any target) as the common workhorses, Extended Absence ({3}{B} exile), Wrath of the Bloodmane ({2}{R} 4 damage, often {1}{R} in this legend-dense set), Violent Echoes and Fulminous Forte at uncommon. Counts by colour: **black 14, red 11, white 7, blue 5, green 5, gold/colourless 18**.

**Set-specific rules.** **Blue does not kill things** — its answers bounce, soft-counter or Pacifism, so blue cannot be a deck’s only interactive colour. **Green’s removal is fight effects**, which need a body and lose to instant-speed removal in response — discount them. **Five removal spells are colour-hosed** (Refute Destiny, Terminal Criticism, Essence Burn, Flourishing Grapple, Precise Redaction): sideboard all-stars, maindeck liabilities. **Echoed pairs mean legends are everywhere** (32 characters printed twice), so “if you control a legendary creature” clauses are close to free. **Planeswalker-matters cards** should be judged against having exactly one Jace token, which is what most decks will actually have.

## Format brief — everything that isn't a single card

Reality Fracture is a ten-archetype format built on two shared engines and an unusually cheap
answer pool. Jace Beleren's Echoverse gives every colour a way to build the same planeswalker
token, every allied pair a recurring free spell at common, and every colour pair a dual land at
common. The result is a format where fixing is nearly free, splashing is cheap, and the games are
decided by whether you answered the right threat and whether anyone attacked the Jace.

### ⚠ This brief has no play data

Captured 2026-09-21, four days before the prerelease and eleven before release. There is no
17Lands GIH WR, no win-rate table, no measured pick order. Everything below is either a **count**
taken from full set data, or a **pre-game prediction** from a published reviewer. The two are
labelled where it matters, and the counts are the part to trust. Rewrite this brief once real
data lands.

### The ten archetypes

There are ten two-colour archetypes, not five. The allied pairs are the colleges of Hexhaven; the
enemy pairs are built around the Echoverse versions of major characters. All ten have a signpost
and all ten have a common dual land.

| Pair | Name | Plan | Signpost | Removal | 2-drops | Avg MV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B/R | Stingerquill | Face burn, noncombat damage | `Grim Repriser` | **26** | 12 | 3.10 |
| W/B | Liliana's Attrition | Small creatures dying for value | `Twisted Fates` | 23 | 11 | 3.10 |
| B/G | Garruk's Bestiary | Deathtouch trades, creature value | `Primal Witchstalker` | 21 | 11 | 3.28 |
| U/B | Theorix | Graveyard math, threshold at seven | `Recursive Recruitment` | 20 | **14** | **3.01** |
| R/W | Ajani's Army | Go-wide, +1/+1 counters, Cadets | `Warrior's Blades` | 20 | 13 | 3.23 |
| R/G | Konstrari | Heartwood ramp into big creatures | `Craftwork Crusher` | 18 | 15 | **3.39** |
| U/R | Chandra's Prowess | Noncreature spells matter | `Clash of Elements` | 17 | 15 | 3.11 |
| G/W | Vigorbloom | Lifegain into counters and cards | `Bloombrute` | 13 | 15 | 3.35 |
| W/U | Fatehold | Surveil aggro, cheap fliers | `Desperate Futurescribe` | 13 | **16** | 3.07 |
| G/U | Jace's Mastery | Empower Jace, planeswalker value | `Mind Meanderer` | **11** | 16 | 3.27 |

**The pick is B/R.** It has the most removal of any pair and no colour has more at common than
black or red. Its weakness is the curve — it is light on two-drops for a deck that wants to
attack, and black has the fewest two-drops at common of any colour. If the two-drops aren't
there, black's removal is just as good in U/B, which has the most.

**The trap is G/U.** It has the least removal of any pair, its signpost is a six-mana flier that
fights on entry, and the loyalty it needs comes from cards every other drafter wants as well.
Take the Jace pieces for whatever deck you end up in and leave the pair alone.

Three more that read differently than the table suggests:

- **W/B is a removal deck with a sacrifice angle, not a sacrifice deck with removal.** Draft it as
  black removal plus white bodies. Don't plan to race — few pairs are lighter at two mana.
- **U/B is the cheapest pair and deepest at two mana**, and it is the one pair whose enablers and
  payoffs genuinely feed each other. The cost is the wait: before the seventh card hits the
  graveyard, none of the threshold bonuses are switched on.
- **R/G carries the highest curve in the format** and only gets away with it because Heartwood
  tokens ramp and its expensive commons carry basic landcycling.

### Where the removal is

Sixty removal spells: black 14, red 11, white 7, blue 5, green 5, and 18 gold or colourless. At
common the gap narrows — red 4, black 3, green 3, white 2, blue 2 — so the black-and-red
advantage is real but concentrated at uncommon.

**Blue does not kill things.** Its answers bounce a creature, tap it, or strip its abilities. A
blue deck needs a second colour that can actually kill, and that is the single most reliable
deckbuilding constraint in the format.

**Green's answers are fight effects.** They need a body already on board and they are card
disadvantage into an opposing removal spell. Count them at a discount.

Five spells are colour-hosed, and the rates are premium precisely because the conditions are
punishing: `Refute Destiny` (green or blue), `Terminal Criticism` (blue or red), `Essence Burn`
(black or green), `Flourishing Grapple` (red or white), `Precise Redaction` (white or black).
These are sideboard cards that steal games — board them in hard once you know the matchup.

Twenty-eight removal spells cost one or two mana and twenty-two are instants, so both players
have interaction. Three damage kills 68% of creatures and the step to four damage buys nineteen
points more. Thirty-two percent of creatures have toughness four or greater, which is why
conditional removal keyed to big bodies is live more often than it reads.

### Engine one: the Jace token

Thirty-five cards empower Jace, eleven of them at common, spread across all five colours. This is
not a blue mechanic — it is a colourless one that happens to make a blue token.

The rule that makes it matter: **you only ever have one Jace token, and every empower card feeds
the same one.** Five separate cards reading "Empower Jace 2" build a single ten-loyalty
planeswalker. No payoff card is required, only volume. The token surveils for one loyalty and
draws a card for three.

Three interactions are worth more than the token's own abilities:

- **It turns on the mana.** All ten common duals enter untapped if you control a planeswalker. An
  early Jace fixes the rest of the game.
- **`Compel Brutality` turns it into removal.** Its second mode has a planeswalker you control
  deal damage equal to its loyalty.
- **`Silence the Echo` eats a spent token.** It wants a creature or planeswalker sacrificed, and a
  drained Jace is ideal fodder.

Cheapest loyalty at common: `Arcane Amphisbaena` and `Academic Ascent` for two, `Campus Crier`
from the graveyard for one, `Protege's Awakening` for six loyalty at four mana.

**Attack the Jace.** A token left alone plausibly decides more games than a two-drop does, and
most opponents will leave yours standing because it doesn't threaten the board.

### Engine two: Prepared

Twenty-four cards, ten at common. A prepared creature carries a spell on its other face; while
prepared you may cast a free copy, which unprepares it. Each allied pair owns one spell, and that
spell is the pair's plan in miniature — `Peer Review` (W/U, a 2/2 Cadet and surveil),
`Omit Variables` (U/B, mill three), `Vicious Verse` (B/R, 1 damage to an opponent), `Soul Tether`
(R/G, a Heartwood token), `Seed Suture` (G/W, a +1/+1 counter and 1 life).

The commons enter prepared and fire once. **Three uncommons re-prepare at your upkeep whenever
they aren't, so they fire every turn for the rest of the game:** `Stingerquill Voxmancer`,
`Paradox Shaper`, `Woodwork Prodigy`. In a long game those are the strongest engines available,
and they cost one to three mana.

### The mana

Ten common dual lands, one per pair, each entering untapped if you control a planeswalker. Add
basic landcycling for two mana on big commons in four colours, plus `Room of Refuge` and
`Murmuring Volume` as colourless fixers. **A third colour for one removal spell is affordable**,
and you should be readier to splash than instinct suggests. Sequencing matters: playing a cheap
empower spell before the dual is often worth a full turn.

### The draft plan

1. **Removal first.** `Last Gasp` and `No Admittance` ask nothing of you. `Silence the Echo` wants
   a sacrifice or three more mana. `Compel Brutality` wants a body. `Surgical Precision` wants a
   target with toughness four or greater.
2. **Then the cheap fliers and the deathtouch bodies**, then cards that are two bodies in one.
3. **Then read which pair's prepared creatures are wheeling.** They signal what's open more
   reliably than the gold cards do, because every deck in those colours wants them.
4. **Walk in wanting B/R** and move off it only when the two-drops don't show.

### Sealed and deckbuilding doctrine

Find the bombs first, then the removal, then let those two choose your colours. A reasonable
curve is one or two one-drops, seven or eight twos, five or six threes, three or four fours, two
or three fives, at most one six, and seventeen lands. Slower decks push that up, aggressive decks
pull it down.

Specific to this format:

- **Never run blue as your only interactive colour.**
- **Count green's fight effects at a discount** when you're deciding whether you have enough
  answers.
- **Take the self-preparing uncommons highly in Sealed specifically.** Sealed games go long and a
  free spell every turn compounds; in a fast draft deck they're merely fine.
- **Splash freely** given the fixing, but only for removal or a bomb.
- **Play around instant-speed removal in every colour.** White's `Prophesied End` kills anything
  for two at instant speed, and it draws its controller a card only if the creature wasn't
  attacking — so attacking into it is the cheaper line.

### Where the sources disagree

- **Removal density versus raw power.** The per-pair counts point at B/R. The reviewer grades
  cluster their top scores in **red and green** — five of the nine perfect scores are one or the
  other. If a pool hands you two red or green mythics, believe the bombs over the archetype table.
- **G/U.** One source calls it the format's trap on removal count; the official archetype guide
  presents it as a normal deck. The count is the more reliable signal.
- **Prepared's ceiling.** One source treats the self-preparing uncommons as major engines, another
  grades them as solid-but-unexceptional. Both readings survive: strong in a long game, mediocre
  in a short one, and nobody yet knows which kind of game this format produces.

### Open questions the data can't settle

- **Format speed.** The averages say normal — mana value 3.2, 68% of spells at three or less — but
  averages have been wrong about speed before, and speed decides whether the grindy graveyard pair
  is real.
- **Whether Jace is a build-around or a rider.** Every colour can empower. Nobody knows yet
  whether decks that lean in beat decks that take the free loyalty and move on.
- **How much the colour-hosed removal actually costs you.** In a diverse field it's a liability;
  in a field that settles on black and red it's close to unconditional.
- **Whether the echoed-pair legends matter mechanically** or are just flavour. Several cards check
  for a legendary creature, and with 32 characters printed twice the density is high enough that
  those checks may be effectively free.

<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/2/1/2185c08f-bb4d-49d5-8b6c-c629a48bb61c.jpg?1789556729" width="240" alt="Sanctum Lurker" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Sanctum Lurker</b><br><sub>B · Rare</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 2.5 · AZ 4.0</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Grade this up. A 3/2 for three is fine on its own; the growth clause only matters if you&#x27;re already deep in empower cards, and the {6} activation is a mana sink you&#x27;ll rarely afford. Filler outside a committed G/U build.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> Inspired Tethermage is a great card to draw later in the game, as it provides a good amount of late game inevitability, but playing it early sounds pretty atrocious. Starting out as only a 3/2 is very poor, and the main way to trigger it is to empower, which you’ll need to do some other way.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> Mana sinks just don’t inspire me the way they used to. Cards are so efficient and packed with value now that I’m treating that part more like bonus upside than a reason to draft this.</sub></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/6/b/6b8789a6-3b63-4198-af5f-c2f2f49fafd9.jpg?1789470736" width="240" alt="Puppet Crafting" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Puppet Crafting</b><br><sub>G · Rare</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 3.0 · AZ 3.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Build-around rare, unplayable outside R/G. Heartwood tokens turn it into a two-mana 5/5 that still taps for mana, and the graveyard recursion insures against the two-for-one. With no artifacts or enchantments in your pool it&#x27;s a sideboard card, so don&#x27;t move in on it early.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> Getting Ensoul Artifact back into Standard is a very interesting concept. That card was extremely powerful when it was first printed, and I reckon we’ve got the tools available to make it good again this time.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> Ensoul Artifact used to be a busted Constructed card. This is basically a juiced-up version of that effect, just in a color that’s a lot less naturally interested in having piles of artifacts lying around. Green does at least have plenty of enchantments to work with.</sub></td>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/3/5/3546b93b-a7d1-451d-a369-22cc8ddcd00d.jpg?1788865848" width="240" alt="Restore with Empathy" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Restore with Empathy</b><br><sub>G · Uncommon</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 2.0 · AZ 2.0</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Narrow role-player. Instant-speed regrowth on any permanent is real card advantage but does nothing early and needs something already dead. The four life makes it a live enabler in G/W Vigorbloom; elsewhere it is a 23rd card at best.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> I’m a huge fan of Pulse of Murasa . It’s a card I’ve cast a lot in Pauper and won games on the back of. Spending 3 mana just to get something back from the graveyard is not usually a winning proposition, but gaining 4 life is a great buffer to help you stay alive having done so.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> A Regrowth that can only grab permanents is obviously a little limited, but in green that’s usually what you were planning to get back anyway. What pushes this up for me is the instant speed and the four-life tacked on.</sub></td>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/7/c/7c725702-8696-4e5a-8318-62f5e2616d52.jpg?1789470857" width="240" alt="Simulacrum Shaper" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Simulacrum Shaper</b><br><sub>G · Rare</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 3.5 · AZ 4.0</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Solid role-player, a touch under the grade. Three mana for a 2/2, a tapped land, and a card when it dies is fine value, but fixing is close to free here with ten common duals, so you&#x27;re paying for ramp and a replaceable body. Best in R/G, where the extra land finds real top-end.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> If we’re going to ramp on turn 3, it might as well be with Simulacrum Shaper . The classic Solemn Simulacrum always felt a little over-costed, but at 3 mana it’s absolutely perfect. A creature that Rampant Growth s on turn 3 has proven itself time and time again, but drawing a card when it dies is an absurd upgrade.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> Solemn Simulacrum has been a great card in both Limited and Constructed for about a billion years. Now you’re telling me I get a cheaper version? Sounds like a bargain to me.</sub></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/0/2/02ee7817-40af-4fcf-a2df-eb218b669281.jpg?1788878199" width="240" alt="Something Worth Saving" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Something Worth Saving</b><br><sub>G · Common</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 2.0 · AZ 2.0</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Marginal filler that does nothing to the board. It replaces itself only if a permanent is in the top four, and the gain-one is noise. The mill matters in U/B threshold and B/G, where it&#x27;s a fine 22nd card; anywhere else it&#x27;s the first cut.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> It may not be in the Theorix colors, but Something Worth Saving is a great way to fill your graveyard. It replaces itself immediately while loading four cards into your graveyard, and you won’t find many enablers better than that.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> This does a bunch of little things that can add up to something pretty useful in the right deck. You get some card selection, a little graveyard filling in a format with plenty of ways to profit from that, and a life gain trigger thrown in for good measure.</sub></td>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/b/6/b635389c-e286-4edb-80d1-23dbe4a18857.jpg?1789614751" width="240" alt="Sureshot Sower" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Sureshot Sower</b><br><sub>G · Common</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 1.5 · AZ 2.0</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Solid green common and better than a 1.5. A 3/1 reach two-drop trades up early and holds off the fliers this format uses to break stalls, then converts to a hard answer for a flier late when it&#x27;s stopped attacking. Green wants exactly this shape.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> A 2-drop 3/1 is great for putting pressure on opposing Jace tokens, and reach also lets Sureshot Sower block really well. When you draw it late it’ll get a lot worse, but the ability to discard it and destroy a flying creature gives it a great extra purpose when you get to that point in a game.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> Normally, “destroy target creature with flying” is code for “please leave me in the sideboard until further notice.” Sureshot Sower gets to dodge that fate because it’s still a perfectly acceptable two-drop when your opponent forgot to bring any birds, dragons, angels, or other airborne nonsense.</sub></td>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/8/b/8be5ee47-8f8a-4e3c-b1a1-9ca0e1fdec7f.jpg?1789127270" width="240" alt="Tarmogoyf" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Tarmogoyf</b><br><sub>G · Mythic</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 2.5 · AZ 3.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Solid green two-drop, not the mythic its name implies. By turn four it&#x27;s usually a 2/3 or 3/4 for two, which beats most bodies it meets, but it has no evasion, no text and no reach — it stops mattering exactly when the format&#x27;s fliers take over. Good early pick, never a bomb.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> Ma BOI! I’ve only been able to make it to the Pro Tour once in my career and Tarmogoyf is one of the cards responsible for helping me get there.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> Oh, how the mighty have fallen. There was a time when Tarmogoyf showing up across the table made people start reconsidering their life choices. Now we’re looking at it in Limited and saying, “Yeah, that’s a pretty good two-drop.” It’s still going to be a whole lot of stats for the low, low price of two mana.</sub></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/3/8/38589a7c-9cfb-4bcc-845e-9dc205095853.jpg?1789129937" width="240" alt="Tethermage&#x27;s Advantage" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Tethermage&#x27;s Advantage</b><br><sub>G · Common</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 0.5 · AZ 1.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Near-last pick. One mana for +2/+2 and an untap is a genuine ambush blocker and it can steal a race, but it is still card disadvantage in a format where repeatable value breaks stalls. Sideboard against fliers; cut it from most maindecks.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> Even at 1 mana, combat tricks just aren’t good enough in green unless they can do a lot more than just +2/+2. If you’re really short on removal, then Tethermage&#x27;s Advantage could make the cut, but there are so many better cards I hope I never have to.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> Do you need a cheap combat trick and mostly just care about getting some extra stats? Cool, this does the job. The reach and untap clauses will absolutely matter from time to time, but they also tempt you into casting this during combat while your opponent is sitting there with open mana and a suspicious amount of conf…</sub></td>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/2/b/2bb7a8eb-227f-410b-859f-750ef0aea2f0.jpg?1789644841" width="240" alt="Verdant Kraken" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Verdant Kraken</b><br><sub>G · Rare</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 5.0 · AZ 4.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Bomb, with a real cost. Seven mana and triple green keeps it out of splashes, but a 6/6 that adds a 3/3 land creature every single upkeep — including the opponent&#x27;s — ends the game about two turns after it resolves. If you&#x27;re green, this is your first pick.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> This bomb rare is a reference to Verdant Force , an extremely powerful rare in its own right. Verdant Kraken is a lot better, creating much more relevant tokens for 1 mana less.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> I’ll be real here: I am very close to giving this a 5.0. The only things holding me back are the seven-mana price tag and the fact that, if you’re not careful, your opponent can still kill it before you get any value. Make no mistake, though—this card is absolutely cracked.</sub></td>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/e/5/e5ed142b-2b61-4ef5-8b23-2db2a0a0319d.jpg?1789556814" width="240" alt="Vinelasher Adept" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Vinelasher Adept</b><br><sub>G · Common</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 1.5 · AZ 2.0</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Late-pick with a floor. Six mana for a 2/4 body plus three counters is clunky value that does nothing if they kill the target in response, and the reach is the best part of the statline. Landcycling means it&#x27;s never dead. Twenty-third card in green; cycle it more often than you cast it.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> This looks like the weakest of the landcyclers, but it can still pack a punch. Of course, the main reason to play Vinelasher Adept at all will be to fix your mana, but if you end up playing it, sticking three +1/+1 counters on a creature is still a strong effect if you can find a good window for it.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> I’m putting this right alongside the other low-end basic landcyclers. On raw rate, it’s the kind of top-end card you only really consider when your deck is running out of better options.</sub></td>
</tr>

<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/3/d/3d693cb0-681e-480a-8f70-07e94c39225c.jpg?1789385843" width="240" alt="Wrecking Gecko" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Wrecking Gecko</b><br><sub>G · Common</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 0.5 · AZ 1.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Draftsim&#x27;s 0.5 is simply wrong. It&#x27;s clunky and the firebreathing is fake, but this is a real green common, not a sideboard card.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> There are a plethora of great ramp targets for Konstrari decks to play. Naturally, as a common, Wrecking Gecko is the worst by a lot. Your average green deck isn’t interested in what’s essentially just a 5/5 vanilla creature, and most ramp decks will be able to find something better.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> I guess this is what happens when you ignore the Gecko and don’t save 15% on your car insurance. <td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/d/a/dad6afc9-8505-4cdd-bf79-e9ba4670f2bb.jpg?1789127966" width="240" alt="Edgar, Moonlit Sovereign" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Edgar, Moonlit Sovereign</b><br><sub>G · Uncommon</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 3.0 · AZ 3.0</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Solid uncommon with a real floor. The &#x27;didn&#x27;t cast a spell&#x27; clause is awkward, so value it as a good body with upside, not an engine.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> Seeing Edgar Markov reimagined as a werewolf in the Echoverse is pretty sweet. Most of the power of Edgar, Moonlit Sovereign comes from the ability to flash it in and eat an attacker in combat.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> Apparently, Edgar switched from Team Edward to Team Jacob. I could keep going with the Twilight jokes, but my wife reads these and it’s not worth the debate when I know which team she is on.</sub></td>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/2/8/28fbb55a-5c9d-45ee-bf42-a84b1048f5d2.jpg?1789127976" width="240" alt="Fblthp, Knows the Way" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Fblthp, Knows the Way</b><br><sub>G · Uncommon</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 3.0 · AZ 2.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Trap at 3.0. In a normal two-colour deck this is a */2 that pays X to draw you lands you didn&#x27;t need — fixing is already free here with ten common duals, and the power ceiling wants a greedy four-colour mana base that&#x27;s worse than just playing a clean deck. Weak body, expensive.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> Finally, a version of Fblthp who thought to bring a map with him.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> I’ll start by saying that I’m genuinely happy for Fblthp. </tr>

<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/9/0/90ca5812-ceb5-46bd-b049-aed7ff10e6af.jpg?1788329370" width="240" alt="Garruk, Curse Breaker" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Garruk, Curse Breaker</b><br><sub>G · Mythic</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 5.0 · AZ 5.0</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Bomb, first pick out of any pack. Splash him if you have to.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> This new Garruk is a great throwback to the original Garruk Wildspeaker . Each of the abilities are very similar to the original’s, but amplified to match the extra mana that Garruk, Curse Breaker costs. On top of that, we get a free Garruk&#x27;s Uprising , which makes all the difference.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> Hey look, another planeswalker that generates card advantage while protecting itself. At this point, that seems to be the easiest way to earn a 5.0 in this set. A 4/4 trampler for five mana that draws you a card when it enters would already be a perfectly playable Limited card.</sub></td>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/1/d/1d535b5f-c916-4f16-89a7-9477578826d2.jpg?1788878290" width="240" alt="Ghalta the Unstoppable" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Ghalta the Unstoppable</b><br><sub>G · Uncommon</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 2.0 · AZ 2.0</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> High ceiling, brick floor. Late playable in R/G only.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> Ghalta the Unstoppable has all the same issues as its white counterpart, but with one key upside. <td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/f/5/f5a0bb3e-8119-4739-8684-e61d1d607dcb.jpg?1789014406" width="240" alt="Jiang Yanggu, Never Alone" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Jiang Yanggu, Never Alone</b><br><sub>G · Uncommon</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 2.5 · AZ 3.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Solid playable everywhere in green. Four mana for five stats across two bodies plays well on both sides of the board, and the untap clause quietly means Heartwood tokens make mana on your turn and still untap for theirs. Above-average, not a card to build around.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> And peace is restored. Jiang Yanggu, Never Alone and his best friend Mowu, together as they should be.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> I’ve already said how much I love cards that give you more than one reasonably sized body, and this one goes a step further by giving you a total of 5/5 worth of stats for four mana. That’s just a really good rate.</sub></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/3/c/3cfa4fc6-4d90-4576-a83f-6496c7f21104.jpg?1789614764" width="240" alt="Loot, the Nexus" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Loot, the Nexus</b><br><sub>G · Uncommon</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 3.0 · AZ 2.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Marked down from 3.0. It&#x27;s a 2/1 for three that dies to everything and only ramps once you already have a diverse board — by which point you want threats, not mana, and this format&#x27;s ten common duals have already solved your fixing. Modest R/G ramp filler.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> Mana dorks at 3 mana tend to be a little underwhelming, but if they tap for more than 1 mana they really mean business. Loot, the Nexus is only guaranteed to tap for 1 mana, but with the potential to tap for 2, 3, or even more, it stands out as a premium green uncommon, particularly in Konstrari.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> Are you playing multicolor shenanigans? Then go ahead and bump this little dude up because he can fix for basically anything. He can even double-ramp you early as long as you have another creature with a different power, which can lead to some pretty gross starts. Would I like him more at two mana? Of course.</sub></td>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/9/0/90f33f99-7bc5-42e1-815e-bfb4c2b74107.jpg?1789644564" width="240" alt="Marwyn, the Preserver" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Marwyn, the Preserver</b><br><sub>G · Uncommon</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 2.5 · AZ 2.0</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> The body is the whole card, and it&#x27;s a fine one. A 3/2 for two attacks past most early blockers, but the hexproof and land recursion are effectively blank in Limited. Green is deep in two-drops, so this is a good-not-great playable rather than a priority pick.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> We can ignore the first ability, because it has no relevance in Reality Fracture from what I can see. A 3/2 for 2 mana is a decent size for a creature already, and if you’re able to fill up your graveyard, getting to draw a land from your graveyard for 2 mana is a very powerful ability.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> If only they had printed an Evolving Wilds in this set. Alas, you’re probably going to have to mill a land or two if you want to squeeze any extra value out of Marwyn. Making your lands hexproof is about as exciting as it sounds in Limited, which is to say it’s probably not coming up very often.</sub></td>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/f/f/ff0bc30f-9d20-458e-808f-bdc2825905a5.jpg?1789387120" width="240" alt="Pia, Aether Ascetic" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Pia, Aether Ascetic</b><br><sub>G · Uncommon</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 2.0 · AZ 1.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Filler. The tutor is only live if you drafted an enchantment worth finding, and most pools have zero to two, so this is usually a three-mana 2/2 with a discard outlet stapled on. Playable if green is short; nothing to prioritize.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> You can’t always run Pia, Aether Ascetic , but this set has quite a few powerful enchantments, including the cycle of “Way” enchantments and multiple removal spells. If you have enough good targets for it, you can definitely run this as a way to find them.</sub><br><sub><b>🅰 AZ:</b> This is dangerously close to unplayable if your deck doesn’t have any enchantments to support it. If you do, though, Pia can be a perfectly solid contributor.</sub></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/e/e/eed83302-dc2c-45f4-a4bd-af9da51edef5.jpg?1789358701" width="240" alt="Ruric Thar, Magecrusher" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Ruric Thar, Magecrusher</b><br><sub>G · Uncommon</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 3.5 · AZ 2.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Legitimate top end, not an expensive vanilla. Hexproof until it connects means removal can&#x27;t answer it before it swings, and reach plus vigilance plus trample covers both sides of a stall. Seven mana is the cost; R/G Heartwood ramp is how you pay it. A real trick in B/G.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> WotC keeps printing these cards in one form or another, and I’m never impressed by them. <td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/7/a/7a44581f-8fc4-457d-888a-1e211090ee7e.jpg?1789470870" width="240" alt="Frostbite Pyromental" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Frostbite Pyromental</b><br><sub>RU · Rare</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 0.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Fringe rare despite the stats — a three-mana hasty 4/4 trample that draws two is only that if it connects, and any 2/2 blocker reduces it to a three-mana Nothing. <td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/8/2/8295c48c-b4dd-4bc1-a206-04cf12b79bbd.jpg?1789470746" width="240" alt="Grim Repriser" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Grim Repriser</b><br><sub>BR · Uncommon</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 2.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Above its grade. <td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/7/d/7d29dfa1-9582-47bc-8f42-62b611bdcc4e.jpg?1789127645" width="240" alt="Konstrari Charm" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Konstrari Charm</b><br><sub>GR · Uncommon</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 1.0</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Bottom-of-the-deck R/G filler, though 1.0 is a touch low. <td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/2/d/2d6ff182-a853-4898-895b-072c89324ca7.jpg?1788878236" width="240" alt="Kwia Vigorbloom" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Kwia Vigorbloom</b><br><sub>GW · Mythic</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 5.0</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Bomb, full stop. <td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/9/4/94c290ce-252c-42b3-bcb0-c1ef621df566.jpg?1789470861" width="240" alt="Mind Meanderer" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Mind Meanderer</b><br><sub>GU · Uncommon</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 3.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Strong card, weak home. <td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/3/a/3afdc75a-1bf5-4f2f-84eb-d82f77a095cd.jpg?1789127648" width="240" alt="Null Summoner" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Null Summoner</b><br><sub>BU · Rare</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 3.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Strong U/B rare. <td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/c/f/cf0eec8c-0475-4050-8144-481a9bb13a0f.jpg?1789127661" width="240" alt="Proctor of Potential" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Proctor of Potential</b><br><sub>UW · Rare</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA — · DS 3.5</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Aggressive and hard to kill permanently. An 0/4 for two blanks the aggressive two- and three-drops, it counts as an artifact for Pia and Craterclaw Colossus, and the eight-mana sacrifice is a real late-game answer to a bomb. Late pick, real playable.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> I instinctively want to say this is bad, but a 0/4 does actually block for your Jace tokens pretty well and can then deal with an annoying creature in the late game. Only playable when you&#x27;re splashing two or three off-colour cards and need the extra land count.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> Mana rocks have been performing well in recent sets due to their additional abilities getting considerably better than they used to be.</sub></td>

Two mana for a colourless 1/3 blocker that fits any deck; bring it in against a deck built entirely on entry triggers.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> It’s quite funny that Karn, Argent Defender looks like a great card to get off of Karn, the Great Creator . A 5/4 trample for four outclasses the format&#x27;s common creatures, and any creature-dense deck casting a spell most turns keeps him untapping. Discount him only if your curve is light on creatures and artifacts.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> A 5/4 trampler for just 4 mana hits incredibly hard. Needing you to cast a creature or artifact spell to untap it is a pretty big downside, but unlike the original Traxos, Scourge of Kroog , Traxos, Scourge Eternal at least enters untapped, so you get that first attack without needing to cast another spell.</sub></td>
<td width="33%" valign="top"><img src="https://cards.scryfall.io/large/front/e/e/ee609b68-5c9c-43e0-aff4-eb1bbc8b2911.jpg?1789060230" width="240" alt="Emrakul, the Exigent Doom" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><br><b>Emrakul, the Exigent Doom</b><br><sub>C · Mythic</sub><br><sub>GIH <b>—</b> · IWD — · ALSA —</sub><br><sub>OH — · GD — · Play —</sub><br><br>🤖 <b>AI:</b> Unplayable in draft. Ten mana is out of reach even for R/G Heartwood ramp, and the exile-for-mana mode turns it into an overpriced Rampant Growth rather than a threat. Sideboard it; the only realistic home is a Sealed pool with heavy acceleration and nothing else to do.<br><br><sub><b>📝 DS:</b> I guess we’re heading into an Eldrazi storyline for 2027, and I’m all here for it! Sadly, as cool as Emrakul, the Exigent Doom is, it isn’t worth trying to cast at all. Ten mana is, well, untenable.</sub></td>
